title: Teacher Education Without the Education Establishment
author: Davis Smith
summary: Davis Smith, a classical humanities teacher and Hillsdale graduate, presents Hillsdale College as a model for teacher education outside state certification and national accreditation. He revisits Daniel Coupland's 2012 account of why Hillsdale resisted Michigan's accreditation mandate and criticizes CAEP standards for giving little weight to content and pedagogical knowledge. Instead of an education major, Hillsdale requires future teachers to complete its core curriculum and an academic major, with a 19-credit minor in classical education. Courses such as English Grammar, Philosophy of Education, Explicit Phonics Reading Instruction and Classical Pedagogy anchor the program. Hillsdale has extended the model to a graduate school of classical education and a leadership master's for practicing educators. Smith concludes that this approach shows teacher preparation can thrive without the mandates of the education establishment. The piece is advocacy from an alumnus and should be read that way.
points: Hillsdale left state certification and national accreditation to align teacher preparation with its liberal arts mission.
Smith criticizes CAEP's standards for devoting only one of seven to content and pedagogical knowledge.
Future teachers major in an academic subject and take the core curriculum instead of an education major.
A 19-credit classical education minor covers grammar, philosophy of education, explicit phonics and classical pedagogy.
The model has grown into graduate programs that prepare teachers and leaders for classical K-12 schools.
quotes: Indeed, Hillsdale College resists (what Whalen terms) “the bureaucracy of experts” that dominates mainstream teacher preparation.
Of its seven standards required for “initial” accreditation, only one is devoted to “content and pedagogical knowledge.
Rather, it required future teachers to complete a rich and rigorous core curriculum and to major in an academic subject just like any other student at the college.

One required course is English Grammar, which prepares teachers to understand and communicate the structure of language at a deep level, enabling their students to develop clear and polished communication.
Another core course is Philosophy of Education, which uses classic texts to delve into perennial questions about the nature and purpose of the educational task.
Examples of electives include Explicit Phonics Reading Instruction, which tackles the nation’s literacy crisis head-on through learning the traditional method of sounding out phonemes

Graduates of these programs are equipped not only to teach but also to serve as school leaders, policy advisors, curriculum developers, and other important roles in the renewal of classical K-12 education.
